newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Coffee extends rally to new 18-month high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee extends rally to new 18-month high.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures surged to new 18-month highs Wednesday, boosted by roaster hedge buying and further fund speculation, traders said.
The move extends a four-week rally, fueled by low consumer stocks and a bullish supply outlook, analysts said.

"There's been heavy buying by uncovered coffee roasters during what is a seasonal supply dip at this time of year, while the news about the strike in Colombia has also fueled bullish sentiment," Merrill Lynch director of commodity research Bill O'Neill, said.

CSCE nearby active March arabica coffee futures were up 7.20 cents early afternoon Wednesday at 170.75 cents a pound, after seeing a new contract high at 171.00 cents. The May through to December 1997 delivery months also saw new contract highs.
On the London Commodity Exchange, March robusta coffee futures were up $26 a tonne at $1651, after seeing six month highs Tuesday at $1680.

CSCE March coffee remained above its five-day (weekly) and 21-day (monthly) simple moving-averages, but oscillators suggested the contract may be over-bought again, requiring a pullback before further gains, analysts said.
The supply/demand situation remained bullish, analysts said.
"The latest data has been mixed and overall there is little sign that coffee stocks will be increasing very much," Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said.
"The most bullish factor in the market has been the decline in coffee stocks in consuming countries," he said.

The Green Coffee Association reported that as of December 31, U.S. stocks were 1.327 million bags, up 63,000 bags from November as the Mexican crop harvest in late 1996 allowed supplies to increase. Subsquently Mexican coffee exports in January, at 130,476 60-kg bags, were reported to be 17 percent ahead of year-ago levels.
But CSCE stocks remained very low at only 15,769 bags Tuesday, analysts noted.

"Until now roasters have been buying on a just-in-time basis only but they are now being caught by a potential supply shock with consumer stocks very low, the late 1996 crops well absorbed and the prospect of a low Brazilian crop ahead this year," Refco New York analyst Anne Prendergast said.
Low consumer stocks have seen the nearby spreads become sharply backwardated, with the CSCE March/May spread jumping to contract highs at 7.25 cents a pound Wednesday.
With wholesale coffee prices up around 45 percent in the past six weeks, retailers have started to raise prices also.

Procter and Gamble's Folgers Coffee Co said Tuesday it planned to raise the list price on its standard 13-ounce can of coffee by 15 cents effective March 17, due to higher prices of green coffee on the world's futures markets.
Earlier bullish estimates of a smaller-than-usual 1996/97 Brazilian coffee crop of around 19 million bags, plus heavy rain in coffee growing regions, helped fuel the rally.

But the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) put the Brazilian crop around 23 million to 24 million bags, while former USDA agricultural attache and industry consultant Leon Yallouz, estimated a higher 28 million-bag crop, according to a report seen by traders in New York.

The ACPC met in Brazil in January and agreed to withold 1.3 million bags of robusta coffee and 300,000 bags of arabica coffee under the group's export retention scheme, limiting ACPC member arabica exports to 24.98 million bags in the first half of 1997.
Brazil would withhold an additional 140,000 bags, Colombia 100,000 bags and central American producers around 60,000 bags, analysts said.

Concerns about the impact of a Colombian state workers strike which began Tuesday were also fueling bullish sentiment, analysts said. Labor leaders billed the strike of 800,000 public sector workers as the biggest in 20 years, which may disrupt exports from the second largest exporter of coffee.
--New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641
